title: This Bird Smears Rotten-Smelling Goo on Her Eggs, and It Protects Them
subject: hoopoe bird

scenes.text: A mother bird coats her own eggs in something that smells like rotting meat.
She's a hoopoe. During nesting, a gland near her tail swells and makes a dark brown oil.
The oil is full of living bacteria, mostly a kind called Enterococcus.
She rubs it onto the eggs, The shells have tiny pits. By hatching, almost 90 percent of those pits are packed with bacteria.
Why? Those microbes make antibiotics. Scientists think they shield the embryo from harmful germs trying to seep through the shell.
The eggs start out pale blue and turn muddy brown. The smell isn't a flaw. It's the armor.

description:
A mother hoopoe coats her eggs in a dark, foul-smelling oil full of living bacteria.
Those bacteria make antibiotics, and scientists think they shield the embryo inside the shell.
Would you want to live in a nest that smells like that? Tell us below.
